— critical at 6 years At six years old, the iPhone 11 series battery is the single most common repair we see on these devices. Six years of daily charge cycles leaves most batteries well below Apple's 80% service threshold — and many significantly below that. At this level of degradation, iOS performance throttling is active, the device feels noticeably slower, and battery life may be measured in hours rather than a full day. Check Settings → Battery → Battery Health. Below 80% is Apple's service recommendation. Below 70% — common on heavily used 6-year-old devices — the device may shut down unexpectedly at 20–30% charge, charge slowly, or generate significant heat during charging. Battery replacement on the iPhone 11 series is the single best-value repair available — restoring full performance, removing throttling, and extending daily life dramatically. Same-day replacement available at our Silvamonte centre. ⚠ OLED burn-in — common at 6 years on heavy-use devices The Super Retina XDR OLED panels on the iPhone 11 Pro and 11 Pro Max are showing burn-in on heavily used devices at this age. OLED burn-in occurs when the same image is displayed at high brightness for extended periods — the organic compounds in the OLED pixels degrade unevenly, leaving a permanent ghost image visible particularly on light or white backgrounds. Common burn-in patterns on iPhone 11 Pro: Ghost of the status bar (time, signal bars, battery icon) visible as a faint permanent overlay. Ghost of the keyboard visible at the bottom of the screen. Navigation bar ghosts on white backgrounds. Burn-in is permanent — it cannot be corrected by software or settings. Screen replacement with a new or used original OLED panel resolves it. We also offer OLED glass-only refurbishment if the panel is working but the glass is cracked without significant burn-in. ⚠ Hydra charging IC failure — Lightning charging fault at this age The iPhone 11 series uses the Hydra IC (the successor to the Tristar U2 chip used on earlier models) to manage all Lightning charging communication, USB authentication, and power delivery. After six years of daily use — particularly if cheap, non-MFi certified Lightning cables have been used — the Hydra IC fails at a significant rate on this generation. Symptoms of Hydra IC failure: "This accessory may not be supported" with Lightning cables that worked previously Won't charge at all — cable plugged in, nothing happens, no charging icon Won't charge on Lightning but charges wirelessly — this is 80% Hydra IC, 20% charging port Doesn't appear in iTunes / Finder when plugged into a computer Very slow charging — draws minimal current despite a working cable and adapter Overheating near the Lightning port during charging attempts Won't turn on at all — in severe Hydra failure, the phone cannot boot because the Hydra IC manages I2C data lines that the backlight driver and bootloader depend on Cause: Cheap, uncertified Lightning cables — particularly cables bought at petrol stations, market stalls, or bundled with non-Apple accessories — do not include the correct E75 authentication chip that Apple's Hydra IC expects. Without this handshake, the unfiltered current from the charger reaches the Hydra IC directly, causing progressive damage and eventual failure. A single power surge through a cheap cable can kill the IC immediately. This is a micro-soldering repair — the Hydra IC is removed under microscope and replaced. We perform this regularly on the iPhone 11 series. Free diagnostic before any work is quoted. ⚠ TrueDepth camera damage — very common on iPhone 11 series, specialist repair TrueDepth camera damage and Face ID failure is one of the most common iPhone 11 and 11 Pro repairs we see. The TrueDepth system comprises multiple components — dot projector, infrared (IR) camera, flood illuminator, and earpiece/sensor flex cable — and any one of them failing produces the same result: Face ID unavailable. How iAssist repairs TrueDepth camera faults — JCID tag on flex: We use the JCID tag method on the flex cable to repair TrueDepth camera faults on the iPhone 11 series. This specialist technique reads and writes the authentication data associated with the TrueDepth components, allowing the Face ID system to be restored after flex cable damage or component replacement — without the need for an original paired donor assembly. If the repair is viable, Face ID is fully restored to normal operation. When the JCID method cannot fix it — IR camera failure: If the infrared (IR) camera itself has failed, no flex repair or JCID tag method can restore Face ID. The IR camera on the iPhone 11 series is cryptographically paired to the device at the factory — it cannot be swapped from another phone or replaced with a new unit. If the IR camera is the fault, Face ID cannot be recovered on that device. We diagnose this specifically during our TrueDepth assessment and tell you clearly before charging anything. Price: R1,500 — if the fault is repairable via JCID flex tag, across all iPhone 11, 11 Pro, and 11 Pro Max models. If the IR camera is confirmed as the fault and Face ID cannot be recovered, there is no charge for the diagnostic. If your iPhone 11 lost Face ID after a screen replacement at another shop, or if it has gradually stopped working — bring it in for a free TrueDepth diagnostic. We assess, confirm whether it is repairable, and quote before any work begins. ⚠ No SIM / No Service — Transceiver IC fault iPhone 11 models are increasingly presenting with baseband and No SIM faults at this age. The most common board-level cause is failure of the Transceiver IC (XCVR_K — PMB5765) on the logic board. This chip manages cellular radio transmission and reception. When it fails, the iPhone shows "No SIM Installed" despite a working SIM, or loses all cellular service permanently. Additional causes include the inductor FL8442 at the bottom of the logic board — located near the upper antenna connector and very easily damaged during disassembly. If No SIM appeared immediately after a repair (screen replacement, battery replacement), FL8442 damage during that repair is the likely cause. Both are micro-soldering repairs. We diagnose the exact fault before quoting — free assessment, quote in writing before any work begins. ⚠ NAND storage failure — stuck in iTunes / DFU mode, P15 programmer repair iPhone 11 series devices are coming in regularly with NAND-related failures — and this is one of the most mishandled repairs in the industry. The NAND flash storage chip has a finite number of read and write cycles. At six years of daily use — particularly on devices that were heavily used for photos, apps, and frequent iOS updates — the NAND chip develops worn sectors, bad blocks, and degraded read/write speeds that cause the device to fail in ways that look like software problems but are not. What many shops get wrong: When an iPhone 11 is stuck in iTunes or DFU mode and restore keeps failing, the most common response at general repair shops is to repeatedly attempt DFU restores — sometimes charging for a "software repair" — without ever diagnosing the underlying hardware cause. A NAND failure cannot be resolved by any software restore. The restore fails because the NAND chip cannot complete the write process reliably. Attempting more restores does not fix this and wastes the customer's time and money. Common symptoms of NAND failure on the iPhone 11 series: Stuck in iTunes / recovery mode — device shows the USB cable and iTunes/Finder logo. Restore starts but fails with error codes 4013, 9, 14, or 21. Progress bar begins then the restore aborts. DFU restore loop — device enters DFU mode, restore begins, fails with the same error code every attempt. Extremely slow performance — the device is inexplicably sluggish even after a battery replacement. App launches take 30–60 seconds. iOS feels unresponsive. The NAND is failing to serve read requests at normal speed. Bootloop that software cannot fix — device restarts continuously; no amount of restoring resolves it. The repair — NAND replacement using the P15 programmer: We use the P15 NAND programmer to replace and correctly program the NAND chip on the iPhone 11 series. This specialist tool reads and writes the device's unique identifier data — serial number, Wi-Fi MAC address, and baseband information — from the original NAND and programs it into the replacement chip. Without correct programming via a tool like the P15, the replacement NAND will not allow the device to activate. This is the difference between a properly executed NAND replacement and a device that restores but cannot connect to Apple's servers. Storage upgrade to 256GB — recommended when replacing NAND: Since the board is already open and the NAND micro-soldering work is being performed, we strongly recommend upgrading the storage to 256GB at the same time. The NAND chip is the primary cost — upgrading the capacity adds minimal cost relative to the total repair while giving the device a fresh chip with maximum remaining write cycles and significantly more storage. Many iPhone 11 series devices came in 64GB or 128GB configurations where storage was already a limitation. If your iPhone 11 is stuck in iTunes or DFU mode and restore keeps failing — this is almost certainly a NAND issue, not a software problem. Bring it in for a free board-level diagnostic. We assess the NAND, discuss the repair and 256GB upgrade option, and quote before any work begins. storage capacity for extended periods. The NAND chip has a finite number of read/write cycles, and when it begins to fail the device presents with symptoms that look like software problems. What many shops get wrong: Repeated DFU restores charged as "software repair" without diagnosing the hardware fault. A failing NAND cannot be fixed by any restore — the restore itself fails because the NAND cannot complete the write process. Error codes 4013, 9, 14, or 21 during restore, or DFU loops that never complete, point to NAND. The repair: NAND chip replaced using the P15 NAND programmer , which correctly programs the replacement chip with the device's unique identifiers. We recommend upgrading to 256GB when replacing NAND — the board is already open and the upgrade cost is minimal relative to the total repair. If your iPhone 12 Mini is stuck in iTunes or DFU mode with repeated restore failures — bring it in for a free board diagnostic before attempting more software restores. ⚠ Motherboard weakness — baseband and Wi-Fi failure from board flexion The iPhone 12 Mini has a well-documented board-level weakness that is directly related to its size. To fit the A14 chip, 5G modem, RF components, and all supporting circuitry into the 5.4" chassis, Apple used the smallest logic board in the 12 series — and one of the most compactly packed boards of any iPhone to date. The consequence is that the board has significantly less mechanical rigidity than the boards in the standard 12 or 12 Pro. What happens: The compact board flexes under load — from drops, from pressure applied when opening the device, or simply from the chassis twisting slightly over years of daily use. This micro-flexion causes the solder joints on the RF section of the board — particularly the baseband modem and Wi-Fi / Bluetooth chip connections — to crack. The failure presents as: No SIM Installed — despite a confirmed working SIM card. Cellular service drops completely. No Service / Searching — signal permanently lost even in areas with full coverage on other devices. Wi-Fi greyed out — Wi-Fi toggle is missing or greyed out entirely and cannot be enabled. Bluetooth greyed out — Bluetooth disappears from Settings alongside Wi-Fi. Wi-Fi and cellular both fail simultaneously — a combined failure pointing to the shared RF section of the board rather than individual component faults. When it happens: Most commonly after a drop (even a minor one), after a screen or battery replacement where the chassis was opened and the board flexed slightly, or on heavily used devices after extended daily use. The 12 Mini's board has less tolerance for flexion than any other current iPhone — making the repair process itself a risk factor if performed without proper chassis support. The repair: Pad inspection and reball of the baseband modem and/or Wi-Fi chip connections under microscope. The affected solder joints are reflowed with fresh solder. We use a board holder to support the 12 Mini chassis during all repairs to prevent additional flex-induced damage during the process. In severe cases where the chip itself has been damaged, replacement of the RF IC is required — a more involved repair that we assess and quote before proceeding. screen — AB adhesive failure and exposed display flex The iPhone 14 Pro and 14 Pro Max have a well-documented display fault caused by the failure of the AB adhesive (acrylic-based optical bonding) that holds the display panel assembly together. This is one of the most common issues we see on these models and requires specific understanding to explain correctly. What happens: The iPhone 14 Pro and Pro Max use a tightly laminated "sandwich" display structure — the OLED panel, touch digitiser, and protective glass are all bonded together in layers using AB adhesive. Over time, and particularly when exposed to heat cycles, humidity, or steam, this adhesive dries out and begins to contract. As it contracts, the OLED display frame starts to lift away from the physical panel underneath it. When the frame lifts, the display flex cable — the ribbon that carries all display signals from the logic board to the OLED panel — becomes exposed . An exposed flex has no protection from moisture, movement, or pressure. Once exposed it begins to corrode, bend, or crack, producing the characteristic symptoms: Bright green screen — entire display shows solid green with no image Yellow screen or yellow tint — display image visible but with strong yellow cast Vertical or horizontal lines — green, purple, or white lines running across the display No display at all — flex cable corrosion has progressed to the point of complete signal failure Flickering — intermittent flex connection producing a flickering or strobing display Partial display failure — one portion of the screen works correctly while another shows discolouration or no image This fault is progressive — it typically starts as an intermittent green tint or yellow cast, particularly at low brightness or in warm environments, and worsens over time as the adhesive continues to contract and the flex continues to degrade. Do not wait to bring it in. Why it happens on 14 Pro and Pro Max specifically: The ProMotion Always-On Display on these models runs continuously — 24 hours a day — generating heat cycles that accelerate AB adhesive degradation faster than on models where the display turns off completely. It is damaged by hard drops — especially when the back glass breaks — or after an incorrect back glass repair. Generates panic code 0x100000 . Presents as random rebooting every 2–5 minutes. 15 series introduced the most aggressive parts pairing Apple has ever implemented on an iPhone. Both the display assembly and the battery are now cryptographically paired to the device's serial number and iCloud account. This has significant implications for repair that every iPhone 15 owner should understand. Display pairing: A used or refurbished original Apple screen from a donor iPhone 15 is almost always paired to that donor phone's iCloud account. This makes it locked to its previous owner — it cannot be transferred to another device without the original owner's Apple ID credentials. This means that "used original Apple" screens, which were a cost-effective repair option on previous iPhone generations, are frequently unusable on iPhone 15 models. Any non-paired display will show an "Important Display Message" notification, and the True Tone and colour calibration data cannot transfer correctly without Apple's System Configuration tool — which requires Apple authorisation to run. Battery pairing: Standard replacement batteries on iPhone 15 models show an "Unable to verify this iPhone has a genuine Apple battery" message and may report health inaccurately. At iAssist we use decoded batteries that communicate with the iPhone's pairing system one-to-one with the original — no "unknown battery" message, accurate health reporting, and full battery data displayed correctly in Settings. No compromises on battery transparency after your repair. What this means for repair cost: Because used original Apple screens are often locked and unusable, iPhone 15 screen repairs are driven toward new aftermarket OLED screens — which are priced higher than equivalent parts for previous generations. This is a deliberate Apple design decision that increases repair cost at independent shops. We are transparent about this: we will always tell you exactly which screen type we are fitting, what the pairing status is, and what notifications you may see after the repair. How iAssist solves the parts pairing problem: When we replace a screen on any iPhone 15 model, we transfer the correct paired components from your original screen to the replacement display. This is the only way to ensure no "unknown parts" or "unable to verify" error message appears after the repair. This component transfer process adds time — allow 2–3 hours for an iPhone 15 screen replacement. The extra time is not optional. Skipping the transfer is what causes the persistent error message customers experience at shops that do not perform this step. Parts pairing affects iPhone 15 and all later models. When you book a screen replacement at iAssist, the component transfer is included — no error messages, no unknown parts warnings. ⚠ Camera lens weakness — cracks easily on the 15 and 15 Plus The iPhone 15 and 15 Plus have a known weakness in the rear camera lens covers. The protective glass over the 48MP main camera and Ultra-Wide camera cracks more easily than on previous generations — particularly the main lens, which sits prominently in the redesigned camera housing. Even placing the iPhone face-up on a rough surface can crack the lens cover. The redesigned camera bump on the iPhone 15 shifts how the device sits and where contact points are — leading to higher lens cracking rates than the 14 series in daily use. A cracked lens cover does not necessarily mean the camera module is damaged — if photos still look sharp in the centre, lens replacement alone is the right repair. We assess first before recommending full camera module replacement. Camera lens protectors are strongly recommended for the iPhone 15 and 15 Plus. ⚠ Random rebooting — panic log diagnostics, R250 assessment Random rebooting on the iPhone 15 and 15 Plus follows the same hardware flex cable pattern as earlier iPhone generations. We read the iOS panic log file first to identify the exact error code before replacing anything. R250 diagnostic — credited toward the repair if you proceed. Causes and panic log codes: Back glass / wireless charging flex — code 0x400000 The flex bonded to the back glass carries the wireless charging coil signal. Damaged by drops or back glass repair. SMC PANIC code 0x400000 . Device restarts every 3 minutes after back glass is disturbed. Proximity flex — code 0x200000 Runs along the top of the device alongside the TrueDepth assembly. Easily liquid-damaged or torn during a screen replacement. Panic code 0x200000 . 3-minute restart cycle — typically starts after screen repair or water exposure near the top speaker. Charging port flex — code 0x100000 The USB-C bottom flex integrating the charging connector, barometer, and microphone sensors. Damaged by hard drops, especially when the back glass breaks. Panic code 0x100000 . Random reboots every 2–5 minutes. Also presents as "Missing sensor: prs0" (barometer) in the panic log text. Battery fault — code 0xa1 A defective or severely degraded battery can trigger random restarts. Panic code 0xa1 . Check Settings → Battery → Battery Health. Battery replacement resolves this. How to find your panic log: Settings → Privacy → Analytics & Improvements → Analytics Data → scroll to files starting with "panic-full" → open the most recent file. Look for "SMC PANIC - ASSERTION FAILED" and the sensor array value. A software restore does nothing for hardware flex bootloops. Bring it in for a panic log diagnostic — we identify the exact fault before touching any part. ⚠ USB-C charging failure — IC fault or charging port The iPhone 15 series was Apple's first USB-C lineup and the USB-C charging circuit is a known failure point across all models. Cheap, non-certified chargers and power surges through the cable are the primary cause. The chips involved: U2 Charging IC / USB-C Controller (Main): SN2012027 — often referred to as 8N or 8N Q4EE. This is the primary USB-C controller that manages Power Delivery negotiation with the cable and charger. EEPROM IC (Paired): 8N — often paired with the SN2012027 to form a cryptographically linked set, sometimes referred to as U9720 in schematics. If either chip is damaged, both must be replaced together from the same donor board. Quick diagnostic — charges wirelessly but not via USB-C cable? This points directly at the USB-C charging circuit. In our experience: ~80% of the time it is the USB-C IC , and ~20% of the time it is the physical USB-C charging port . Both caused by a cheap charger or power surge through the cable. Avoid charging from desk ports, car USB-C outlets, and built-in furniture chargers that do not properly implement USB-C Power Delivery. booking ⚠ Parts pairing — iPhone 15 is the first year Apple paired both screen AND battery to iCloud The iPhone 15 series introduced the most aggressive parts pairing Apple has ever implemented on an iPhone. Both the display assembly and the battery are now cryptographically paired to the device's serial number and iCloud account. This has significant implications for repair that every iPhone 15 owner should understand. Display pairing: A used or refurbished original Apple screen from a donor iPhone 15 is almost always paired to that donor phone's iCloud account. This makes it locked to its previous owner — it cannot be transferred to another device without the original owner's Apple ID credentials. This means that "used original Apple" screens, which were a cost-effective repair option on previous iPhone generations, are frequently unusable on iPhone 15 models. Any non-paired display will show an "Important Display Message" notification, and the True Tone and colour calibration data cannot transfer correctly without Apple's System Configuration tool — which requires Apple authorisation to run. Battery pairing: Standard replacement batteries on iPhone 15 models show an "Unable to verify this iPhone has a genuine Apple battery" message and may report health inaccurately. At iAssist we use decoded batteries that communicate with the iPhone's pairing system one-to-one with the original — no "unknown battery" message, accurate health reporting, and full battery data displayed correctly in Settings. No compromises on battery transparency after your repair. What this means for repair cost: Because used original Apple screens are often locked and unusable, iPhone 15 screen repairs are driven toward new aftermarket OLED screens — which are priced higher than equivalent parts for previous generations. This is a deliberate Apple design decision that increases repair cost at independent shops. We are transparent about this: we will always tell you exactly which screen type we are fitting, what the pairing status is, and what notifications you may see after the repair. How iAssist solves the parts pairing problem: When we replace a screen on any iPhone 15 model, we transfer the correct paired components from your original screen to the replacement display. This is the only way to ensure no "unknown parts" or "unable to verify" error message appears after the repair. This component transfer process adds time — allow 2–3 hours for an iPhone 15 screen replacement. The extra time is not optional. Skipping the transfer is what causes the persistent error message customers experience at shops that do not perform this step. Parts pairing affects iPhone 15 and all later models. When you book a screen replacement at iAssist, the component transfer is included — no error messages, no unknown parts warnings. ✅ Back glass — no laser machine required on 15 Pro and 15 Pro Max For the first time since the iPhone 8, the iPhone 15 Pro and 15 Pro Max have a back glass that can be removed without a laser machine. Apple changed the internal chassis design on the titanium Pro models, allowing the back glass to be carefully removed using heat and controlled separation — the same basic technique used on older pre-12 iPhones. This is a significant improvement for repairability. On iPhone 12, 13, and 14 models, back glass replacement requires a precision laser to vapourise the adhesive — a specialised machine that not all repair shops own, and that adds cost and time to the repair. On the 15 Pro and Pro Max, the process is faster, simpler, and less expensive. The result: back glass repair on the iPhone 15 Pro and 15 Pro Max is faster to perform and priced more favourably than on equivalent 14 Pro and 14 Pro Max models. ⚠ Random rebooting — panic log diagnostics, R250 assessment Random rebooting on the iPhone 15 Pro and 15 Pro Max has multiple hardware causes. We read the iOS panic log file first and identify the exact fault code before replacing anything. R250 diagnostic — credited toward the repair if you proceed. Causes and panic log codes: Wireless charging flex — code 0x400000 The flex cable that wraps around the logic board and carries the wireless charging coil signal. If disconnected, damaged, or defective it generates SMC PANIC code 0x400000 and causes 3-minute restart cycles. Common after back glass repair or a hard drop. Proximity flex — 3-minute restart A damaged or disconnected proximity flex causes 3-minute restart problems on the 15 Pro. Easily damaged by liquid or torn during a screen replacement on the titanium chassis. Charging port flex — random restarts The USB-C port flex. Damaged by drops, especially when the back glass is cracked. Causes random reboots every 2–5 minutes after the device is disturbed. Battery fault — code 0xa1 A defective or failing battery causes random restarts with panic code 0xa1 . Specifically documented on the 15 Pro Max — the device restarts every 3 minutes when the battery is bad. Check battery health and connector pins before assuming a flex cable fault. How to find your panic log: Settings → Privacy → Analytics & Improvements → Analytics Data → scroll to files starting with "panic-full" → open the most recent file. Look for "SMC PANIC - ASSERTION FAILED" and the sensor array value to identify the faulty component. Always use OEM or premium quality replacement flexes — aftermarket flexes have a high defect rate and can themselves cause the same reboot symptoms. We keep known-good OEM test flexes on the bench specifically for this diagnostic. ⚠ USB-C charging failure — IC fault or charging port The iPhone 15 series was Apple's first USB-C lineup and the USB-C charging circuit is a known failure point across all models. Cheap, non-certified chargers and power surges through the cable are the primary cause. The chips involved: U2 Charging IC / USB-C Controller (Main): SN2012027 — often referred to as 8N or 8N Q4EE. This is the primary USB-C controller that manages Power Delivery negotiation with the cable and charger. EEPROM IC (Paired): 8N — often paired with the SN2012027 to form a cryptographically linked set, sometimes referred to as U9720 in schematics. If either chip is damaged, both must be replaced together from the same donor board. Quick diagnostic — charges wirelessly but not via USB-C cable? This points directly at the USB-C charging circuit. In our experience: ~80% of the time it is the USB-C IC , and ~20% of the time it is the physical USB-C charging port . Both caused by a cheap charger or power surge through the cable. Free diagnostic confirms which before any work is quoted. Always use Apple or MFi-certified USB-C cables and chargers. Avoid charging from desk ports, car USB-C outlets, and built-in furniture chargers that do not properly implement USB-C Power Delivery. Previously, every iPhone from the iPhone X onwards opened from the front, meaning the display had to be removed to access the battery, cameras, logic board, and other internal components. This design change is genuinely positive for repairability. Battery replacement, rear camera work, and other internal repairs no longer require screen removal as a first step — reducing the risk of screen damage during unrelated repairs, shortening repair time, and keeping costs more manageable. It also means that if your screen is cracked, we can still access the internals safely without risking further screen damage. ⚠ Camera Control button — complex to replace individually The Camera Control button — Apple's new touch-and-click interface on the right side of every iPhone 16 — is one of the most complex individual components to replace on these models. The button integrates a capacitive touch layer, a physical click mechanism, and a dedicated flex cable, all housed in a precision-machined slot in the chassis frame. When the Camera Control button fails from a drop or damage to the right side of the device, individual button replacement is very difficult. At iAssist we typically take one of two approaches depending on the extent of the damage: Enclosure / midframe swap — where the button slot itself is deformed or the damage is significant, we replace the complete enclosure or midframe. All components are migrated to the new housing and parts pair correctly — no error messages after repair. Used original midframe — where we have stock of a used original midframe in the correct colour and storage configuration, we use this as the donor housing. All paired components transfer correctly. Camera Control repairs pair fine after the housing swap — no issues with the capacitive surface, click mechanism, or iOS Camera Control functionality. It is not a quick job, but the result is correct. ⚠ Logic board flex at the bottom — baseband and Wi-Fi faults The iPhone 16 series has a new logic board design where the board is more susceptible to flexing at the bottom section. A hard drop, significant pressure, or even aggressive back glass repair can cause the bottom portion of the board to flex enough to disrupt solder joints — producing faults that look like component failures but are actually mechanical connection issues. Common consequences of board flex on the iPhone 16: No baseband / No SIM / No Service — the RF components at the bottom of the board lose connection, presenting as "No SIM Installed" or permanent No Service with a working SIM card Wi-Fi and Bluetooth failure — wireless chip connections disrupted by board flex, presenting as greyed-out Wi-Fi or constant disconnections Ripped pads — where the flex has been severe enough, solder pads physically tear from the board surface, requiring micro-soldering pad reconstruction before any reflow can be attempted These are board-level micro-soldering repairs. We assess under microscope first — free diagnostic, quote before any work begins. ⚠ USB-C charging IC failure — stuck at 1%, charging failure, 0.1A draw USB-C charging IC failure is a known issue on this model and one of the most technically involved board-level repairs we do. Understanding the chip architecture explains why it is not a simple swap. The two-chip charging system: SN2012027 (U2) — USB-PD controller: This is the chip that negotiates USB Power Delivery with the cable and charger. It handles the USB-C handshake that tells the charger what voltage and current to supply. When U2 fails, the phone cannot negotiate charging and either refuses to charge or draws only minimal current. 8N/Q4EE EEPROM — cryptographically paired with the U2: This small companion chip stores calibration and authentication data that is cryptographically linked to the U2 at the board level. The SN2012027 (U2) and the 8N/Q4EE EEPROM are a paired set — if you replace only the U2 controller without moving the original EEPROM or reprogramming a new EEPROM with the correct dump data, the phone will typically show a charging logo but draw no current (approximately 0.1A). Both chips must come from the same donor board or the EEPROM must be correctly reprogrammed. U9500 "Tigris" (CP3200B1G0) — primary battery charger IC: Separate from the U2, the Tigris manages the actual power flow to the battery — the physical charging process. It relies on the U2 for USB-PD negotiation but handles current regulation independently. In some cases the Tigris itself burns out — we have seen this — producing slightly different symptoms to a U2/EEPROM failure. Common symptoms: Stuck at 1%, charging logo shows but phone draws only ~0.1A (visible on USB meter), total charging failure, non-responsive touch during charging, overheating near port. Common causes: Low-quality or incompatible USB-C chargers — particularly older Android chargers, non-MFi cables, and USB-C ports built into desks, furniture, and car dashboards that do not properly implement the USB-C Power Delivery standard. How we diagnose: We assess each case individually — sometimes it is the Tigris (U9500) that has burned, sometimes it is the U2 and EEPROM pair. The symptom presentation and board-level testing tells us which. Specialists use dedicated programmers such as the JCID 16 Series Charging IC Programmer for EEPROM dump and reprogramming where applicable. If your iPhone 15/16 charges normally on a wireless or MagSafe pad but refuses to charge via a USB-C cable, this points directly to the USB-C charging circuit — not the battery. Both are caused by the same root problem — a cheap, non-certified charger or a power surge through the cable damaging the USB-C circuitry. issues on the iPhone 17 Pro Max — read before booking ⚠ Aluminium frame — dents and scratches from minor drops ("Scratchgate") Apple switched the iPhone 17 Pro and 17 Pro Max from the titanium frame used on the 15 Pro and 16 Pro series back to aluminium — and the difference in durability is immediately noticeable in real-world use. The move was made to improve heat dissipation alongside the new vapor chamber cooling system, but the trade-off is a frame that dents and scratches significantly more easily than the titanium predecessor. The issue — widely referred to online as "Scratchgate" — is twofold: Denting from small drops: A minor drop from waist height — even inside a pouch or soft case — can produce a significant corner dent. Users report damage on the very first drop that would have left a titanium or stainless steel iPhone untouched. The soft aluminium deforms on impact in a way that titanium does not. Anodizing chips revealing bare aluminium: The coloured anodized finish on the frame chips off on impact, exposing the silver-grey raw aluminium underneath. On dark coloured models — deep blue, Cosmic Orange — the bare aluminium contrast is very visible. The anodized layer is a surface treatment, not paint, and once the underlying aluminium is exposed it cannot simply be touched up. What iAssist offers: We perform complete frame swaps on the iPhone 17 Pro and 17 Pro Max. All internal components are migrated to a fresh chassis frame — logic board, battery, cameras, flex cables, and buttons — and the device is fully reassembled and tested. A case is strongly recommended for caseless users on this model, but where the damage has already happened, a frame swap restores the device to like-new condition. The vapor chamber distributes heat away from the A19 Pro chip and other hot components far more efficiently than the graphite thermal spreader used in previous iPhone Pro models. This is one of the primary reasons Apple switched from titanium back to aluminium on the 17 Pro — aluminium has significantly higher thermal conductivity than titanium, working in combination with the vapor chamber to manage heat under sustained workloads like video recording, gaming, and Apple Intelligence processing. The practical result is better sustained performance and less thermal throttling during intensive tasks than on the 15 Pro or 16 Pro. ⚠ Opens from the front again — reversed from iPhone 16 series The entire iPhone 16 lineup opened from the back for internal repairs — a welcome repairability improvement. physically damaged, from iPhone 12) R7,500 Face ID repair — IC on MLB Assessment + quote Known issues on the iPhone 17 Pro — read before booking ⚠ Aluminium frame — dents and scratches from minor drops ("Scratchgate") Apple switched the iPhone 17 Pro and 17 Pro Max from the titanium frame used on the 15 Pro and 16 Pro series back to aluminium — and the difference in durability is immediately noticeable in real-world use. The move was made to improve heat dissipation alongside the new vapor chamber cooling system, but the trade-off is a frame that dents and scratches significantly more easily than the titanium predecessor. The issue — widely referred to online as "Scratchgate" — is twofold: Denting from small drops: A minor drop from waist height — even inside a pouch or soft case — can produce a significant corner dent. Users report damage on the very first drop that would have left a titanium or stainless steel iPhone untouched. The soft aluminium deforms on impact in a way that titanium does not. Anodizing chips revealing bare aluminium: The coloured anodized finish on the frame chips off on impact, exposing the silver-grey raw aluminium underneath. On dark coloured models — deep blue, Cosmic Orange — the bare aluminium contrast is very visible. The anodized layer is a surface treatment, not paint, and once the underlying aluminium is exposed it cannot simply be touched up. What iAssist offers: We perform complete frame swaps on the iPhone 17 Pro and 17 Pro Max. All internal components are migrated to a fresh chassis frame — logic board, battery, cameras, flex cables, and buttons — and the device is fully reassembled and tested. A case is strongly recommended for caseless users on this model, but where the damage has already happened, a frame swap restores the device to like-new condition. If you have an iPhone 17 Pro with a dented or scratched frame, bring it in for a free assessment — we quote the frame swap after evaluating the extent of the damage and parts availability. ✅ Vapor chamber cooling — first year on iPhone Pro models The iPhone 17 Pro and Pro Max are the first Pro iPhones to include a vapor chamber thermal system — the same cooling technology used in high-performance Android flagships and gaming phones. The vapor chamber distributes heat away from the A19 Pro chip and other hot components far more efficiently than the graphite thermal spreader used in previous iPhone Pro models. This is one of the primary reasons Apple switched from titanium back to aluminium on the 17 Pro — aluminium has significantly higher thermal conductivity than titanium, working in combination with the vapor chamber to manage heat under sustained workloads like video recording, gaming, and Apple Intelligence processing. The practical result is better sustained performance and less thermal throttling during intensive tasks than on the 15 Pro or 16 Pro. ⚠ Opens from the front again — reversed from iPhone 16 series The entire iPhone 16 lineup opened from the back for internal repairs — a welcome repairability improvement. The iPhone 17 Pro and 17 Pro Max have reversed this, returning to opening from the front for most internal access. The reason is not fully clear, but it is likely related to the new vapor chamber layout and the aluminium chassis structural design requiring different internal access paths. For repair purposes: battery replacement, camera work, and other internal repairs on the 17 Pro again require screen removal as the first step — adding complexity compared to the 16 Pro. The risk of screen damage during unrelated repairs also returns. We factor this into our repair process and turnaround times on the 17 Pro. ⚠ Earpiece flex cable — tears easily, causing no sound during calls The earpiece (top speaker / receiver) on the iPhone 17 Pro sits within the Dynamic Island housing at the top of the device. The flex cable connecting it to the motherboard has proven to be particularly prone to tearing on this model — we are seeing this come through in early units. The earpiece flex runs through a tight path in the top assembly, and any stress from a drop to the top of the device, or from an aggressive screen removal attempt, can tear or sever it. When the earpiece flex tears: The most immediate symptom is no sound during phone calls held to the ear — speakerphone continues to work via the bottom speaker. On the 17 Pro, the earpiece also contributes to the stereo audio spread for media playback, so music may sound noticeably unbalanced. Board-level involvement: If a new earpiece module does not resolve the no-sound issue, or if speaker icons are greyed out during calls, the fault may lie in the interposer connection between the two layers of the sandwich logic board — the audio codec's connection can fracture on drops. This is a micro-soldering repair requiring separation of the logic board layers and reballing of the interposer connection points. Bring it in for a free diagnostic — we determine whether the fault is the earpiece module, the flex cable, or the board-level audio codec connection before recommending any repair. ⚠ Random rebooting — panic log diagnostics, R250 assessment Random rebooting on the iPhone 17 Pro and 17 Pro Max follows the same hardware sensor detection pattern seen across modern iPhone generations. We read the iOS panic log file first and identify the exact fault before replacing any component. R250 diagnostic — credited toward the repair if you proceed. Common causes: Charging port flex — the bottom flex integrating the USB-C charging connector and associated sensors. Easily damaged by water, hard drops, or when a back glass repair is performed with a bad or aftermarket replacement. Causes random reboots every 2–5 minutes or a continuous 3-minute restart cycle. Power button flex — the power/side button flex on the iPhone 17 Pro wraps around the logic board area. A damaged power button flex can send continuous reset signals to power management. Keep a known-good OEM power button flex on the bench for diagnostic testing. Back glass / wireless charging flex — after a back glass repair, the iPhone restarts every few minutes if the wireless charging flex has been disturbed or damaged. Use OEM or premium pull parts only — the flex contains a paired IC. Reading the panic log: Settings → Privacy → Analytics & Improvements → Analytics Data → files starting with "panic-full" → most recent file. Look for "SMC PANIC — ASSERTION FAILED" followed by "Sensor Array" and a value beginning with "23...." — this is the 17 Pro identifier. The specific sensor array value points to which component is at fault. Always replace with OEM or premium quality flexes — aftermarket flexes have a high defect rate and can themselves cause the same restart symptoms, wasting diagnostic time. Used original Apple screens from donor phones are often locked to their previous owner and cannot be transferred. Any unpaired display will trigger an "Important Display Message" or "unknown part" notification. How iAssist handles this: We transfer the correct paired components from your original screen to the replacement display. This prevents any unknown parts message from appearing. Allow 2–3 hours for the component transfer — skipping this step is what causes the persistent warnings many customers experience elsewhere. Component transfer is included in every iPhone 17 screen replacement at iAssist — no error messages after your repair. ⚠ USB-C charging failure — IC fault or charging port USB-C IC failure carries over from the 15 and 16 generation — cheap or non-certified chargers and power surges can damage the USB-C charging circuit. Symptoms: stuck at 1%, won't charge at all, or charges wirelessly but not via cable. Quick diagnostic — charges wirelessly but not via USB-C? ~80% of the time this is the USB-C IC, ~20% the physical port. Both caused by a cheap charger or power surge. Free diagnostic confirms which before any work is quoted. Always use Apple or MFi-certified USB-C cables and chargers. Avoid desk ports, car chargers, and furniture USB-C outlets that do not properly implement USB-C Power Delivery. ⚠ Camera Control button — complex to replace individually Camera Control on the iPhone 17 carries over from the 16 series and remains a complex individual repair when damaged. The touch-and-click button sits in a precision-machined slot in the chassis. A drop to the right side can damage the module, flex cable, or the slot itself. At iAssist we approach Camera Control damage via enclosure or midframe swap where individual button replacement is not viable. Yes — always. iPhone 17 continues the parts pairing introduced on the 15 series. The component transfer from your original screen to the replacement prevents the 'Important Display Message.' Allow 2–3 hours. This is included as standard in every iPhone 17 screen replacement at iAssist. My iPhone 17 charges on MagSafe but not USB-C — SN2012027 or port? ~80% the SN2012027 (U2) USB-C controller IC or its paired EEPROM, ~20% the physical USB-C port. Caused by cheap non-certified chargers. Free diagnostic confirms which. Use Apple or MFi-certified USB-C cables and chargers. What is Camera Control on the iPhone 17 and what happens if it breaks? Camera Control is the touch-and-click button on the right side of the iPhone 17. If damaged from a drop, individual replacement is very difficult. We replace the enclosure or midframe — all components pair correctly after the housing swap. My iPhone 17 restarts randomly — how do I read the panic log? Settings → Privacy → Analytics & Improvements → Analytics Data → panic-full files → most recent. Look for 'SMC PANIC — ASSERTION FAILED' and 'Sensor Array' with a value starting '23...'. R250 diagnostic — we identify the fault before replacing any component. How long does iPhone 17 screen replacement take? Allow 2–3 hours including the component transfer. Same-day service available at our Silvamonte centre. What is the difference between the iPhone 17 and the iPhone 17 Air? The 17 Air is ultra-thin (5.6mm) with a titanium frame, single rear camera, and unique two-layer interposer board. The standard 17 has a more conventional chassis design. Both have Camera Control. The Air is thinner and lighter; the 17 is more repairable. Does the iPhone 17 have a Dynamic Island? Yes — the iPhone 17 has Dynamic Island (the pill-shaped cutout at the top of the screen used for Face ID and Live Activities). The Dynamic Island was introduced on the iPhone 14 Pro and is now on all current iPhone models except the 17e. Is the iPhone 17 worth repairing if something goes wrong early in its life? Yes — the iPhone 17 is a current device with many years of iOS support ahead. Any repair at this age is excellent value. How the iPhone 18 Pro Max's variable-aperture camera works Earlier iPhones use a fixed aperture: the opening that lets light onto the sensor never changes size. The iPhone 18 Pro Max's 48MP Fusion Main camera is different. Apple says its aperture varies from ƒ/1.48 to ƒ/4, adjusted by six laser-cut blades that open and close like the iris of an eye. Apple lists the variable aperture on the main camera only. iFixit's teardown found the blades are a polymer composite roughly as thin as a human hair, and that they're moved by magnets. In photography terms, a wider opening lets in more light and gives a shallower depth of field, while a narrower one keeps more of the scene sharp. Apple pairs the camera with a new computational imaging pipeline. The parts-pairing results are early: one repair-tool company testing one pair of phones. We'll add findings from our own workshop as we repair these phones. Nothing here is guesswork presented as experience. 📷 Variable-aperture camera: repaired as a whole assembly Apple describes the 48MP Fusion Main camera as having a variable aperture from ƒ/1.48 to ƒ/4. iFixit's teardown found six polymer blades roughly as thin as a human hair, moved by magnets, and concluded very few repair enthusiasts will have the tools to take the mechanism apart. Its verdict: if the aperture sticks, you're replacing the entire main camera assembly. The upside is that the camera module itself is modular and easy to reach. What it means for repair: A faulty main camera on the iPhone 18 Pro Max is realistically an assembly replacement, not a repair of the aperture inside it. We confirm at the free diagnostic whether it's the module, the lens cover or something on the board, then quote the part. 🔧 Opens from the front only. The battery is the easy part iFixit reports the 18 Pro and Pro Max open from the front only, as the 17 Pro does, so reaching the battery means lifting the glued-down screen. Once inside, the battery tray is held by screws and the battery uses electrically releasable adhesive that lets go in about 90 seconds at 12 volts. The back glass comes off easily, but the only serviceable part behind it is the wireless charging coil. What it means for repair: Battery, camera and board repairs all start with taking the screen off, so every internal repair carries a screen-damage risk that we plan for. For reference, iFixit measured 4,288 mAh (Pro) and 5,567 mAh (Pro Max) on the eSIM versions, and notes that physical-SIM versions have smaller batteries. 🔌 USB-C port: a step back from the 16 Pro iFixit describes a long flex that runs up the side of the phone to the logic board, with screws and adhesive in the way, and calls getting the port out a chore. It rates this a regression from the more accessible 16 Pro design. What it means for repair: A charging-port repair on the iPhone 18 Pro Max involves more labour than on the 16 Pro. If yours has stopped charging, we start with the cable, debris in the port and the charging circuitry at the free diagnostic, then quote before any work begins. 💾 Storage now sits inside the logic-board sandwich According to iFixit, the A20 Pro chip has moved to the outside of the board sandwich with the RAM beside it, which helps cooling under Apple's larger vapor chamber, while the NAND storage is now inside the sandwich. iFixit says that makes recovery work that needs NAND access more involved. What it means for repair: If your iPhone 18 Pro Max won't switch on and your photos aren't backed up, bring it in for a free diagnostic before trying anything yourself. Board-level repair and data recovery on this generation are more involved than on earlier Pros, and we'll tell you honestly what's possible before you commit. 📺 Display frame and Face ID: the screen is the riskiest repair iFixit found the plastic display frame cracked or peeling in three of its four teardown units and couldn't pin down why. According to CNET's report on the teardown, Apple doesn't sell that frame separately, so a break can mean replacing the whole display module. Separately, the infrared camera used by Face ID has moved beneath the display toward the upper-left, with the selfie camera and dot projector still in the central opening. What it means for repair: A screen replacement on the iPhone 18 Pro Max can change scope once the phone is open, which is why we quote after inspection. Because part of Face ID now sits under the display, damage to the top of the screen can affect Face ID as well as touch and picture. We check Face ID when we diagnose a cracked screen. 🔗 Parts pairing on iOS 27: back glass and cameras easier, the display harder REWA Technology tested two iPhone 18 Pros running iOS 27 in a full parts swap. In Apple's Repair Assistant the display, battery, front camera and rear camera showed as 'Used' after configuration, and the rear camera no longer needed calibration afterwards. The back glass showed no configuration status at all, which suggests it is no longer part of the pairing system, and the battery, enclosure and front camera behaved as they did on iOS 26. The display was different: swapping it together with its sensor flex cables failed configuration and showed an 'Unknown Part' message, and swapping the display alone passed configuration but the message returned once the sensor flex was installed. What it means for repair: A back-glass repair and a rear-camera swap look more straightforward than on earlier models, while a screen replacement on the iPhone 18 Pro Max may show a parts message that earlier iPhones did not. This is early testing on one pair of phones and REWA says it will keep testing, so we'll tell you what to expect at the free diagnostic and update this page as iOS changes. 📶 SIM tray or eSIM-only: it depends where your phone was sold Apple's South African specification lists a physical nano-SIM plus eSIM for the iPhone 18 Pro Max. Assessment + quote What's new on the iPhone 18 Pro — and what it means for repair Everything in this section comes from Apple's published specifications, iFixit's teardown of the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max (20 September 2026, provisional 7/10 repairability score), REWA Technology's iOS 27 parts-swap test (19 September 2026) and press coverage of the teardown. The parts-pairing results are early: one repair-tool company testing one pair of phones. We'll add findings from our own workshop as we repair these phones. Nothing here is guesswork presented as experience. 📷 Variable-aperture camera: repaired as a whole assembly Apple describes the 48MP Fusion Main camera as having a variable aperture from ƒ/1.48 to ƒ/4. iFixit's teardown found six polymer blades roughly as thin as a human hair, moved by magnets, and concluded very few repair enthusiasts will have the tools to take the mechanism apart. Its verdict: if the aperture sticks, you're replacing the entire main camera assembly. The upside is that the camera module itself is modular and easy to reach. What it means for repair: A faulty main camera on the iPhone 18 Pro is realistically an assembly replacement, not a repair of the aperture inside it. We confirm at the free diagnostic whether it's the module, the lens cover or something on the board, then quote the part. 🔧 Opens from the front only. The battery is the easy part iFixit reports the 18 Pro and Pro Max open from the front only, as the 17 Pro does, so reaching the battery means lifting the glued-down screen. Once inside, the battery tray is held by screws and the battery uses electrically releasable adhesive that lets go in about 90 seconds at 12 volts. The back glass comes off easily, but the only serviceable part behind it is the wireless charging coil. What it means for repair: Battery, camera and board repairs all start with taking the screen off, so every internal repair carries a screen-damage risk that we plan for. For reference, iFixit measured 4,288 mAh (Pro) and 5,567 mAh (Pro Max) on the eSIM versions, and notes that physical-SIM versions have smaller batteries. 🔌 USB-C port: a step back from the 16 Pro iFixit describes a long flex that runs up the side of the phone to the logic board, with screws and adhesive in the way, and calls getting the port out a chore. It rates this a regression from the more accessible 16 Pro design. What it means for repair: A charging-port repair on the iPhone 18 Pro involves more labour than on the 16 Pro. If yours has stopped charging, we start with the cable, debris in the port and the charging circuitry at the free diagnostic, then quote before any work begins. 💾 Storage now sits inside the logic-board sandwich According to iFixit, the A20 Pro chip has moved to the outside of the board sandwich with the RAM beside it, which helps cooling under Apple's larger vapor chamber, while the NAND storage is now inside the sandwich. iFixit says that makes recovery work that needs NAND access more involved. What it means for repair: If your iPhone 18 Pro won't switch on and your photos aren't backed up, bring it in for a free diagnostic before trying anything yourself. Board-level repair and data recovery on this generation are more involved than on earlier Pros, and we'll tell you honestly what's possible before you commit. 📺 Display frame and Face ID: the screen is the riskiest repair iFixit found the plastic display frame cracked or peeling in three of its four teardown units and couldn't pin down why. According to CNET's report on the teardown, Apple doesn't sell that frame separately, so a break can mean replacing the whole display module. Separately, the infrared camera used by Face ID has moved beneath the display toward the upper-left, with the selfie camera and dot projector still in the central opening. What it means for repair: A screen replacement on the iPhone 18 Pro can change scope once the phone is open, which is why we quote after inspection. Because part of Face ID now sits under the display, damage to the top of the screen can affect Face ID as well as touch and picture. We check Face ID when we diagnose a cracked screen. 🔗 Parts pairing on iOS 27: back glass and cameras easier, the display harder REWA Technology tested two iPhone 18 Pros running iOS 27 in a full parts swap. In Apple's Repair Assistant the display, battery, front camera and rear camera showed as 'Used' after configuration, and the rear camera no longer needed calibration afterwards. The back glass showed no configuration status at all, which suggests it is no longer part of the pairing system, and the battery, enclosure and front camera behaved as they did on iOS 26. The display was different: swapping it together with its sensor flex cables failed configuration and showed an 'Unknown Part' message, and swapping the display alone passed configuration but the message returned once the sensor flex was installed. What it means for repair: A back-glass repair and a rear-camera swap look more straightforward than on earlier models, while a screen replacement on the iPhone 18 Pro may show a parts message that earlier iPhones did not. This is early testing on one pair of phones and REWA says it will keep testing, so we'll tell you what to expect at the free diagnostic and update this page as iOS changes. 📶 SIM tray or eSIM-only: it depends where your phone was sold Apple's South African specification lists a physical nano-SIM plus eSIM for the iPhone 18 Pro. Apple's US and Nigerian specifications list dual eSIM only, with no physical SIM. iFixit also notes that physical-SIM versions have smaller batteries, so an imported phone can be a different phone inside from one bought locally. What it means for repair: If your phone has a tray, SIM reader and 'No SIM' faults are repairs we can assess. If it's an eSIM-only import there is no tray to fault, and 'No service' is traced through the radio and board. eSIM profiles live on the phone itself, so replacing the logic board (rather than repairing it) would mean your network re-issuing your eSIM. the iPhone 8 — read before booking ✅ Component interchangeability — iPhone 8 shares most parts with SE 2020 and SE 2022 The iPhone 8 is the chassis that Apple based both SE generations on. Screen, frame, charging port, rear camera, speakers, buttons, and Taptic Engine are all interchangeable across iPhone 8, SE 2020, and SE 2022. This means parts are widely available and sourcing is straightforward. Battery — unique per model: The iPhone 8 and SE 2020 share the same 1,821 mAh battery. The SE 2022 uses a larger 2,018 mAh cell — not cross-compatible. Only the batteries and motherboards are unique to each model. Screens — True Tone data transfer required: When swapping screens between any of these three models, the True Tone calibration data from the original display must be transferred to the replacement. We perform this transfer on every screen replacement across iPhone 8, SE 2020, and SE 2022. ⚠ Battery — critical at 8 years At eight years old, iPhone 8 batteries are severely degraded. Most units we see are at 60–75% health — below Apple's 80% threshold by a significant margin. At this level, iOS throttling is aggressive, daily battery life is measured in hours rather than a full day, and unexpected shutdowns at 20–30% charge are common. Battery replacement is the single most impactful repair on the iPhone 8. Check Settings → Battery → Battery Health. Same-day replacement at our Silvamonte centre. ⚠ Back glass — first glass-backed iPhone, laser removal required The iPhone 8 was the first iPhone to use a glass back — required for wireless charging since aluminium blocks wireless charging signals. The glass back cracks easily and requires a laser machine for correct removal. At eight years old, back glass cracks are very common. Cracked back glass does not always stop wireless charging — but severe cracks or missing glass can disrupt the wireless coil. Back glass repair restores the device to full wireless charging function. ⚠ Hydra charging IC — Lightning charging fault at this age The Hydra IC managing Lightning charging fails at this age — particularly from cheap, uncertified Lightning cables used over 8 years. Won't charge on Lightning, "accessory not supported", charges on wireless but not cable. Charges wirelessly but not via Lightning? ~80% Hydra IC, ~20% Lightning port. Free diagnostic confirms which. Use Apple MFi-certified cables only. ⚠ NAND storage failure — stuck in iTunes mode, slow performance, micro-soldering repair After eight years of daily read and write operations, the NAND flash storage chip on the iPhone 8 and iPhone X logic board is increasingly showing wear-related failure. The NAND is the chip that stores iOS, all your apps, photos, messages, and every piece of data on the device. Unlike SSDs in computers, smartphone NAND chips have a finite number of write cycles — and after 8 years of intensive use, many are worn to the point of developing bad blocks, degraded write speeds, and read errors that the bootloader cannot tolerate. Common symptoms of NAND wear on the iPhone 8 and X: Stuck in iTunes / recovery mode — the iPhone enters recovery mode (lightning cable and iTunes/Finder logo on screen) and cannot complete a restore. iTunes or Finder shows error codes 4013, 9, 14, or 21 during the restore attempt. The restore starts, the progress bar appears, then fails. This is one of the clearest indicators of a NAND timing issue — the bootloader cannot read or write to the chip fast enough to complete the iOS installation. Extremely slow performance — even with a brand new battery fitted, the device is inexplicably slow. Apps take 30–60 seconds to open. Every operation involves long waits. This is the NAND struggling to serve read requests at speed. Bootloop that does not resolve with a software restore — the device restarts continuously and DFU restore fails or produces the same error codes repeatedly. Data corruption — apps crash, the OS itself becomes unstable, files become unreadable. The repair — NAND chip replacement (micro-soldering): The original NAND chip must be removed under microscope, the board pads cleaned, and a replacement NAND chip programmed and installed. This requires not just soldering skill but also the ability to correctly program the new chip with the device's unique identifiers (serial number, Wi-Fi address, and baseband data) that are stored on the original NAND. Without correct programming the device will not activate. This is one of the most complex board-level repairs available. Our recommendation when replacing NAND — upgrade to 256GB: If your iPhone 8 or iPhone X is having its NAND replaced, we strongly recommend taking the opportunity to upgrade the storage to 256GB at the same time. The cost of the NAND chip itself is the primary expense — and since the board is already open and the micro-soldering work is already being performed, upgrading from 64GB or 128GB to 256GB adds minimal extra cost relative to the total repair. The result is a device with significantly more storage capacity and a fresh NAND chip with maximum remaining write cycles — effectively extending the useful life of the device considerably. WhatsApp to arrange courier → Common questions iPhone Back Glass Repair — frequently asked questions Why does iPhone back glass repair require a laser machine? The back glass is bonded with very strong adhesive. Mechanical removal risks cracking the chassis or damaging the wireless charging coil. A laser machine safely heats the adhesive to release the glass without collateral damage. What is the OEM quality glass option for iPhone 12 and newer? OEM quality glass matches the original Apple back glass in texture, colour, camera ring alignment, and MagSafe compatibility. It costs R1,000 more than standard replacement glass. Available iPhone 12 through current models. My iPhone 8 back glass is cracked — will wireless charging still work? Minor cracks usually don't affect wireless charging. Severe cracks or missing glass can disrupt the wireless coil signal. Back glass repair restores both glass and full wireless charging function. Does the iPhone 15 Pro back glass require laser? No — the titanium chassis redesign allows removal without laser. This makes back glass repair faster and less expensive than on 14 Pro. My iPhone 14 back glass was replaced and now it restarts every 3 minutes — what happened? The back glass on the iPhone 14 carries a wireless charging flex. If damaged during repair, it triggers panic code 0x400000 — a 3-minute restart loop. Bring it in — we read the panic log and replace the damaged flex. How long does back glass repair take? Most repairs same-day. Laser removal and bonding: 60–90 minutes. OEM glass adds time for correct alignment. Is back glass repair permanent? Replacement glass is the same specification as original. A quality case is recommended after repair, particularly on iPhone 17 Pro series where the aluminium frame is susceptible to denting. Can I use my iPhone after the back glass cracks? The device is functional, but cracked glass exposes the chassis to moisture and further damage. The wireless coil sits directly behind the glass. Wireless charging bypasses the charging IC, which is why wireless works when the IC fails. Free diagnostic confirms which. What is the Hydra IC and why does it fail? The Hydra IC manages all Lightning charging authentication on iPhones 8 through 14. It fails when cheap, uncertified cables are used — they don't include the correct authentication chip, and unfiltered current causes progressive damage. What is the SN2012027 and 8N/Q4EE EEPROM? The SN2012027 is the USB-C Power Delivery controller. The 8N/Q4EE is its cryptographically paired EEPROM. Both must come from the same donor board when replaced. Replacing only the SN2012027 without the correct EEPROM leaves the phone drawing only ~0.1A. Why is charging IC repair on iPhone 16 Pro more expensive? The 8N/Q4EE EEPROM on the 16 Pro sits on the lower layer of the sandwich logic board. Accessing it requires board separation — a precise, time-consuming procedure. My iPhone 15 is stuck at 1% and won't charge past it — is that the IC? Yes — stuck at 1% with cable plugged in is a classic SN2012027 USB-C IC fault. Free board diagnostic confirms before any micro-soldering is quoted. Will my iPhone charge again after IC repair? If the IC is the fault and the board has no secondary damage — yes, full charging is restored. We inspect under microscope for secondary damage before quoting. How do I prevent charging IC failure? Use only Apple or MFi-certified Lightning and USB-C cables. Avoid furniture USB ports, car chargers, and petrol station cables. Does charging IC repair require board removal? Yes — the IC is soldered to the logic board. If the device won't power due to battery or board fault — and the NAND is intact — data recovery is often possible. If the NAND itself is corrupted, recovery becomes harder. Free assessment determines what's possible. Will I lose my data when you replace the NAND chip? The NAND stores iOS and personal data. After NAND replacement using the P15 programmer, the device restores from iCloud or iTunes backup. Local data not in a backup won't be on the device after NAND replacement. I have no iCloud backup — can you recover my photos? If the original NAND chip is still readable, we attempt to boot far enough to perform a local backup before replacing. If too corrupted to boot, access to stored data is significantly limited. We assess honestly — cannot always be achieved. Can you recover data from a water-damaged iPhone? Water damage recovery depends on corrosion extent. Fresh water, brief exposure, brought in quickly — good chance. Salt water, long exposure, charged after — much lower. We clean and assess before advising. What is the P15 programmer and how does it help with data? The P15 reads the device's unique identifiers (serial number, Wi-Fi address, baseband data) and writes them to the replacement NAND chip. Without these identifiers, the device cannot activate on Apple's servers after repair. Can you recover data from an activation-locked iPhone? No. If activation-locked and you don't have the Apple ID credentials — data access is not possible. My iPhone was dropped and smashed — can data be recovered? If the logic board is intact — likely yes. Drop damage typically affects the screen and chassis without damaging the board. We assess board condition, attempt to boot, and discuss options. How long does data recovery assessment take? Same-day initial assessment. In many cases yes — using the JCID tag on flex method. If the fault is in the earpiece/sensor flex, dot projector, or flood illuminator, Face ID can be restored. The TrueDepth system on newer models is more sophisticated and the JCID process more complex. iPhone 15 and 16 series also require additional time for sandwich board architecture. Is there any way to bypass Face ID if it can't be repaired? No. If Face ID is permanently unavailable, a passcode unlocks the device. All other functions continue normally. WhatsApp to arrange courier → Common questions iPhone Frame & Enclosure Repair — frequently asked questions Why does the iPhone 17 Pro frame dent so easily? Apple switched back to aluminium from titanium on the 17 Pro for better thermal conductivity with the new vapor chamber cooling system. Aluminium dents far more easily than titanium — even waist-height drops cause visible corner dents. The anodized finish also chips off on impact. What is a frame swap and what does it involve? A frame swap migrates all your iPhone's internal components — logic board (with all your data), battery, cameras, buttons, and flex cables — into a fresh chassis. All paired components remain on your original board so Face ID, Touch ID, and all functions work correctly after the swap. Is a used original frame the same quality as a new one? Used original frames are genuine Apple chassis from donor devices in good cosmetic condition. They have the correct tolerances, antenna placement, and Camera Control slot precision. New original frames are available at higher cost — we quote both. My iPhone XS stainless steel frame is dented — can that be repaired? Stainless steel is harder than aluminium and more resistant to denting. Minor dents can sometimes be reduced with precision tooling. Significant dents require frame swap to restore structural integrity. Will a frame swap affect Face ID or Touch ID? No — Face ID data is stored on the logic board which moves with you to the new frame. Touch ID is in the Home button flex, which also migrates. All biometric functions fully preserved. How long does a frame swap take? A full frame swap is a significant repair — allow a full day. All components carefully removed, inspected, and re-fitted with appropriate torque and alignment. My iPhone 13 Pro frame is bent after a drop — repair or swap? A minor titanium bend can sometimes be carefully straightened under press. For significant bends, frame swap is more reliable. We assess which is appropriate during the free diagnostic. Is frame swap available for all iPhone models? Yes — across all iPhone models. Parts availability varies by model age. Older models may require sourcing time. A software-caused restart loop is typically resolved with DFU restore in minutes. A hardware-caused boot loop — NAND failure, power management IC fault, or a failing battery unable to deliver peak current — requires board-level diagnosis. Panic logs stored in the iPhone's diagnostic partition record the reason for unexpected restarts. iAssist reads these logs during the free diagnostic to identify the failing component or software process before recommending a repair path. Boot loop — stuck on Apple logo Most common presentation. Could be software or hardware. DFU restore attempted first — if it fails, NAND or board-level fault diagnosis. Random restarts during normal use Spontaneous reboot with no pattern. Panic log analysis identifies the failing process or component — software, NAND, or power management. Restarts when battery reaches low levels Battery unable to deliver peak current demand. Shuts off at 20–30% and restarts. Battery replacement resolves. Restarts while charging Power management IC or charging circuit fault. Restarts specifically during charge cycles. Board-level assessment. Stuck after iOS update Update interrupted or corrupted causing boot failure. DFU restore resolves in most cases. NAND failure if restore itself fails with error codes. Restart loop after repair elsewhere Incorrect component reassembly, damaged flex cable, or power rail short from previous repair. Free assessment determines cause. When DFU restore fails or panic logs point to a hardware source, iAssist diagnoses using a DC bench power supply connected to the battery terminals — the current draw profile at boot identifies short circuits on the power rails before any component is desoldered. We cross-reference against the iPhone schematic (PP_VCC_MAIN, PP1V8, PPVCORE_AP) to isolate the exact failing node. This separates component-level board diagnosis from guesswork. WhatsApp to arrange courier → Common questions iPhone Restart Loop Repair — frequently asked questions My iPhone restarts exactly every 3 minutes — what causes that? thermalmonitord hardware sensor bootloop. iOS reboots when it cannot check in with a required sensor within 3 minutes. The panic log entry reads: 'userspace watchdog timeout: no successful checkins from thermalmonitord — Missing sensor(s): [sensor]'. Reading the panic log identifies the specific component. How do I read my iPhone panic log? Settings → Privacy & Security → Analytics & Improvements → Analytics Data → files starting with 'panic-full' → most recent one → search for 'Missing sensor'. Screenshot it and bring it to us, or we read it during the diagnostic. What does 'Missing sensor: Prs0' mean? Prs0 is the barometric pressure sensor on the charging port flex. Its absence causes the 3-minute restart. Common cause: damaged charging port flex from drops or back glass repair. OEM charging port flex replacement resolves it. What does 'Missing sensor: mic2' mean? mic2 is the secondary microphone on the power/side button flex. Its absence triggers the 3-minute restart. The button may still physically work even when mic2 is missing. OEM power button flex replacement resolves it. Will a software restore fix my iPhone's 3-minute restart loop? No. A hardware sensor bootloop cannot be resolved by any software restore. The sensor must be physically present and communicating. Shops charging for 'software repair' on this fault are not fixing it. What panic log codes apply to the iPhone 14 series? Look for hex codes: 0x400000 (wireless charging flex behind back glass), 0x200000 (proximity sensor flex), 0x100000 (charging port flex). R250 diagnostic — we identify the specific code and component. What is the board escalation for iPhone 11 restart loop? If OEM flex replacements don't resolve it, the fault is in the board. The mic2 I2C lines on the upper sandwich board layer may have ripped pads or shorted capacitors (C7708/C7709). Requires board separation and reball under microscope. Why must OEM parts be used for restart loop repair? Aftermarket button and charging port flexes frequently omit the thermal sensors — cheaper because the sensor components are missing. Can Face ID actually be fixed, or does it mean a new phone? It can usually be restored. The most common cause we see is a previous screen replacement done without the care the dot projector and flood illuminator need — swap the display carelessly and Face ID stops calibrating. It's also not a repair you'll find offered locally in Alberton — this one typically means a drive north or a courier booking. Is there an Apple Store or iStore actually in Alberton? No — there's no Apple-owned store anywhere in South Africa, and no Apple Premium Reseller based in Alberton itself. The nearest iStore locations are at Eastgate Shopping Centre in Bedfordview and East Rand Mall in Boksburg, both a genuine drive from here. My iPhone 15 or 16 is frozen at 1% charge — what's going on? That's the signature of a board-level U9500 charging IC failure — the chip that regulates charging has failed, and touch response sometimes goes with it. None of the shops in Alberton, Germiston or Boksburg work at this level; it requires desoldering and replacing the IC directly on the logic board, plus an EEPROM reflash. My phone's battery seems to drain much faster than it used to — is that just normal wear, or is the commute making it worse? Could well be both. Alberton's a genuine commuter suburb — most residents are driving the M1 North corridor into Johannesburg or Sandton twice a day, and running Maps or a nav app with the screen on and GPS/cellular active that whole time is one of the heaviest everyday battery drains there is. On top of normal age-related wear (most iPhones need a new battery around the two-year mark regardless), that daily load can accelerate things. We test battery health as part of every free diagnostic, so we can tell you honestly whether it's wear, usage, or a bit of both before recommending a replacement. We use OEM-pulled and original-quality displays and OEM battery cells, not generic aftermarket parts — that's why True Tone and colour calibration keep working properly afterwards.
